Keep this sheet open during the labs. It covers every Week 3 concept from Chapter 3, plus origin–destination flow mapping, which the textbook skips (marked \*).

## Key terms

| Term | Means |
|---|---|
| Migration | A change of permanent or semi-permanent residence |
| Immigration / emigration | Moving in / moving out |
| Migrant stock | People living somewhere they were not born, whenever they arrived |
| Migrant flow | Moves during a set period, such as the past year |
| Net migration | In-migrants − out-migrants, often per 1,000 population |
| Diaspora | People who have left their homeland, as a group |
| Refugee | Outside their country owing to a well-founded fear of persecution (1951 UN Refugee Convention) |
| Internally displaced person | Forced from home by conflict, rights violations or disaster, but still inside their country |
| Vulnerability | Susceptibility to harm when exposed to a disaster |
| Intervening obstacle | Anything between origin and destination that slows migration: distance, cost, borders, policy |
| Pioneer migrant | The first to arrive; sends information home |
| Chain migration | Friends and family follow pioneers |
| Cumulative causation | Migration becomes self-sustaining through networks and remittances |
| Remittances | Money migrants send home |
| Migrant selectivity | Movers differ from stayers, above all by age |

## Push and pull forces

| Force | Push (origin) | Pull (destination) |
|---|---|---|
| Economic | Low wages, unemployment | Jobs, higher wages, career growth |
| Social and cultural | Family conflict, discrimination | Family and friends, shared language or religion |
| Political | War, crime, persecution | Safety, democracy, rule of law |
| Environmental | Drought, disaster | Pleasant climate |

Forced and voluntary migration overlap, because insecurity and poverty often go together.

## Distance and size

- **Distance decay:** less migration between places farther apart, because distance adds cost, time and risk. 52% of African migrants and 60% of Asian migrants live in their own region.
- **Gravity model:** flow is proportional to (population A × population B) ÷ distance. Large, close places exchange the most migrants.
- **Cultural distance:** a shared language, religion or colonial history increases flows between distant places.
- **Migration transition:** emigration is low in preindustrial societies, peaks as countries industrialize, then falls as they become wealthy.

## Migrants and health

- The ages of peak migration, late teens to mid-30s, are also ages of high HIV risk.
- Surveys of residents only miss mobile young adults. ACDIS also counts non-resident household members: a third of members lived outside the area in 2006.
- ACDIS HIV survey, 2003–2006: non-resident men had adjusted odds of HIV 1.8 times those of resident men; for women, 1.5 (Tanser et al. 2008).

## Public health case: Dobra et al. 2017

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| HIV-negative adults followed (2000–2014) | 17,743 |
| Geolocated migration events | 8,006, covering over 1 million km |
| Migrated outside the study area at least once | 17.4% |
| Median migration distance | 107 km |
| Distance at which HIV risk rose by 50% | Men 40 km; women 109 km |
| Share of time away at which HIV risk rose by 50% | Men 44%; women 90% |

Main finding: a nonlinear relationship. Even relatively short moves carried substantial added risk.

## Mapping flows\*

**Origin–destination (OD) table:** one row per move or pair of places: origin, destination, count. Keep coordinates or place IDs for both ends.

| To do this | Go to |
|---|---|
| Draw flow lines and measure each move | Analysis → Tools → Connect Origins to Destinations. Choose origin and destination layers, match them by ID, and pick straight-line distance or travel time (uses credits) |
| Show volume as line width | Select the line layer → Styles → choose the count field → Counts and amounts (size) |
| Classify short vs long moves | Styles → choose the distance field → Classify data → Manual breaks (for example at 40 km and 100 km) |
| Map net migration | Add a field and calculate in-migrants − out-migrants; divide by population × 1,000 for a rate |

Sign in at [emory.maps.arcgis.com](https://emory.maps.arcgis.com). Login instructions and free Esri training are on the [Emory GIS resources page](https://gis.ecds.emory.edu/). Esri renames menus from time to time, so if a label differs, look for the nearest match.

## Six questions to ask any migration map

1. Stock or flow? Over what period?
2. Counts, rates or net migration?
3. Which scale: international, national or local?
4. Who is missing: non-residents, the undocumented?
5. Where was the exposure: home or destination?
6. Is distance straight-line or travel time?

## Textbook correction

The "Characteristics of migrants" section credits "Rubenstein" with 1800s migration research. It means E. G. Ravenstein, named correctly earlier in the chapter.
